entries.clue: Jokes ... silences (4)

blocks.note: the plural noun a comedian's act is made of, the material itself
read as a verb instead: stopping a mouth so that nothing more comes out of it

annotation.surface: A comic's material met by the sound of nobody laughing.
annotation.walkthrough: The gap invites you to read one sentence about a routine dying, when the two words are separate definitions standing side by side. The second is a verb, and what it describes is done with a strip of tape.
annotation.definitionFit: The jokes a comedian writes are gags, and to gag someone is to stop their mouth, so the same four letters cover the laughter and the silencing.

entries.clue: To age, getting to grips with a change of home: speed it up! (3,1,4,2)

indicatorNotes.getting to grips with: To get to grips with a thing is to take hold of it all round, so the words before close over the words after.

blocks.note: to get on is to grow older, as in 'he's getting on a bit'
changing address is a move, and the article comes with it

annotation.surface: Somebody elderly wrestling with the upheaval of moving house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To age' reads as a preamble about passing years but is a two-word verb, and it is that verb which splits open. The exclamation mark makes the definition an order, which is how the phrase is nearly always spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: Telling someone to get a move on is telling them to hurry, which is exactly the impatience behind 'speed it up'.

entries.clue: Crushed - then rejoiced, seeing airport staff (6,4)

blocks.note: ground is the past tense of grind, what a mill does to wheat
crew is the old past tense of crow, and to crow is to exult over a triumph

annotation.surface: Someone flattened by news who then finds cause to celebrate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crushed' pulls towards the emotional sense when the miller's is wanted. The other half is the past tense of crow, the form that survives in 'the cock crew'.
annotation.definitionFit: The ground crew are the people who refuel, load and marshal aircraft while they sit on the tarmac, so they are staff an airport cannot run without.

entries.clue: Suddenly exclaims: 'cistern jet's malfunctioning' (10)

indicatorNotes.malfunctioning: A malfunctioning thing has its parts no longer in their proper arrangement, and neither have these letters.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder; the 's is the surface's 'is', not a letter

annotation.surface: A plumber reporting that the lavatory's water jet has gone wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks turn the fodder into something being shouted, which is the very thing the definition describes. Ten letters split across two words is a long run to spot.
annotation.definitionFit: To interject is to break into a conversation with a remark, which is exclaiming and doing it without warning.

entries.clue: One tipped for award? No, Everyman's, in the end, average (7)

indicatorNotes.in the end: In the end points at what a word finishes with, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: the refusal taken as it stands, two letters off the page
this puzzle is signed Everyman, so what is Everyman's is mine
the last letter of average

annotation.surface: Brushing aside a tip for a prize: the man's work is only middling after all.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is the pseudonym the Observer's setter writes under, so 'Everyman's' is this setter's way of saying mine. The question mark admits the definition covers a shortlisting, not a win.
annotation.definitionFit: A nominee is one of the names put forward for a prize, which is the person tipped the moment the shortlist appears.

entries.clue: Relax in East End as that bloke's leaving (4,3)

indicatorNotes.in East End: The East End is working-class London, where the aitch at the front of a word is dropped, so the phrase is heard without it.

blocks.note: he's off is what you say of a man on his way out, and in that accent it loses its aitch

annotation.surface: Telling someone to take it easy now that the fellow in question has gone.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here is an abbreviation or a hidden word: the clue asks you to hear a short sentence spoken in a London accent. 'He's off' is everyday English for he has left.
annotation.definitionFit: To ease off is to slacken the pace and stop pressing, which is what you are being told to do when told to relax.

entries.clue: English playwright, anticipating ham, getting jam, rages madly (5,6)

indicatorNotes.madly: Someone raging madly is past all order, and letters described that way come out rearranged.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, with 'getting' joining the pieces and adding none

annotation.surface: A writer promised ham, handed jam instead, and losing his temper over it.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics on those two three-letter words present them as things on a plate, and they are also six of the letters. Theatre is the surface's world and the answer's too, which keeps the join invisible.
annotation.definitionFit: James Graham is a contemporary English dramatist, the author of Ink, Sherwood and Dear England, so the bare trade and nationality name him.

entries.clue: Is unable to tilt to one side (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The first definition is the contraction can't, and the grid takes it without its apostrophe, as grids always do.

blocks.note: the contraction everyone writes with an apostrophe, which the grid has no square for
a separate word altogether, the one a surveyor uses for a slope off the horizontal

annotation.surface: Something rigid that will not lean over the way it is meant to.
annotation.walkthrough: The sentence has to be cut in two before either half does any work, and the cut falls after the third word. The second half is the builder's word for a slant or a bevelled edge.
annotation.definitionFit: Can't, stripped of its apostrophe, says somebody is unable to; and to cant something is to tip it off the level, two unrelated words that happen to share four letters.

entries.clue: Help! Operetta's overture neither good nor bad (2-2)

indicatorNotes.overture: An overture is the piece that opens a work, so the word in front of it gives up only the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: the distress call, three letters chosen for Morse because nobody could mishear them
the opening letter of operetta

annotation.surface: A cry for rescue at an operetta whose opening music is merely middling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Overture' lives in a world of orchestras while doing the plainest job in cryptics, marking a first letter. The hyphen in the enumeration says the four letters split evenly.
annotation.definitionFit: So-so is the verdict for something that was neither a success nor a disaster, which is the exact middle the definition marks out.

entries.clue: Implement the return of stolen goods (4)

indicatorNotes.the return of: The return of a thing brings it back the way it came, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: stolen goods are loot, and the word comes back the other way

annotation.surface: A police announcement that the proceeds of a burglary have been recovered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The return of stolen goods' reads as property coming back to its owner, which is what disguises the instruction sitting in the middle of it. Four-letter reversals hide well because so little word is left to recognise.
annotation.definitionFit: A tool is any implement taken up to do a job, from a chisel to a spanner.

entries.clue: What'll make you laugh? Met Gala: ultimately, US menswear not half wacky (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a question rather than a noun, and the answer is the plural reply to it: the things that make you laugh.

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so the word beside it surrenders only its final letter.
indicatorNotes.not half: To have not half of a word is to be left without half of it, and menswear keeps four of its eight letters.
indicatorNotes.wacky: Wacky is off-kilter and out of true, and letters called that are no longer in their proper order.

blocks.note: the New York museum whose fashion night this is, three letters straight into the fodder
the last letter of Gala
the two letters as printed
the front half of the eight-letter word

annotation.surface: A fashion writer calling the American menswear at the Met Gala distinctly odd.
annotation.walkthrough: The Met Gala is New York's celebrity fashion night, and keeping those two words together is what stops you seeing where the letters break. 'Ultimately' belongs to Gala alone, not to the pair of them.
annotation.definitionFit: Amusements are the things laid on to divert people, the word a pier uses for its rides and slot machines, so they are what is there for the laugh.

entries.clue: Fellow's playing dance music; one's welcomed in mayoral residence (7,5)

indicatorNotes.welcomed in: Whatever is welcomed in is taken inside, so the letter before it goes among the letters already standing.

blocks.note: a fellow is a man, and the apostrophe-s comes along with him
i is the Roman numeral for one
a show that is playing tonight is on
house is the four-to-the-floor dance music of the clubs

annotation.surface: A man spinning house records at a reception in the mayor's official home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fellow's playing' looks like one verb phrase but is two pieces, the fellow and the 'on' that a show playing tonight is. 'Dance music' wants a genre, and the genre it wants doubles as a building.
annotation.definitionFit: The Mansion House is the Lord Mayor of London's official residence, the Georgian palace facing Bank junction, so the plain phrase is literal.

entries.clue: Memorialist worked to ___ (11)

indicatorNotes.worked: Clay that has been worked has been kneaded into a new shape, and letters worked come out in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, the whole word and nothing else

annotation.surface: A line from a quiz with its last word blanked out.
annotation.walkthrough: The blank is where the answer goes in the sentence, and the sentence's first word hands over every letter of it. A memorialist is one who writes memoirs or raises monuments to the dead.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: what a memorialist labours at is keeping the dead in memory, which is what the missing word names.

entries.clue: Cut-price, pooh-poohed (10)

blocks.note: the shop-window sense, money knocked off the ticket
the other sense entirely, an idea waved away as not worth counting

annotation.surface: A bargain that somebody sniffed at.
annotation.walkthrough: Both readings are past participles, so nothing in the grammar shows where the seam between them falls. To pooh-pooh a suggestion is to wave it away as not worth considering.
annotation.definitionFit: Goods sold discounted are marked down from the ticket price, and to discount a claim is to refuse to count it at all, the same verb pulling two ways.

entries.clue: Forebear enacted ten plays (10)

indicatorNotes.plays: A joint that plays moves loosely about instead of holding still, and letters given that freedom settle somewhere new.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, a verb and a number

annotation.surface: An ancestor who staged ten dramas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plays' sits at the end looking like the noun the sentence needs, and is the verb doing the shuffling. In grammar an antecedent is also the thing a pronoun points back to.
annotation.definitionFit: An antecedent is one who went before in a family line, which is what a forebear is: grandparents and everyone further back.

entries.clue: Very important chap - ou, monsieur très éminent, primarily! (7)

annotation.definition: Very important chap - ou, monsieur très éminent, primarily!

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily means first of all, so every word in the run gives up just the letter it starts with.

blocks.clueFragment: Very important chap - ou, monsieur très éminent
blocks.note: seven words in the order printed, each handing over its opening letter

annotation.surface: Someone insisting in two languages that the man is a person of consequence.
annotation.walkthrough: The French half is not decoration: 'ou' is simply French for 'or', and its one letter is needed as much as the rest. The rank sits between baron and comte in the old French nobility.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a vicomte is a French nobleman ranking above a baron, which is a very important chap described in his own language.

entries.clue: Backing of rule of monarch from another land (7)

indicatorNotes.Backing: Something backing is travelling to the rear, so the word it takes hold of is written out the other way about.

blocks.note: the word 'of' turned round
a monarch's rule is a reign, the years spent on the throne

annotation.surface: The support behind a king's rule coming from abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue prints two 'of's and only the first is a word to be used; the second belongs to the phrase that means reign. In an across entry a reversal runs the letters right to left.
annotation.definitionFit: A foreign visitor, coin or policy is one belonging to a country other than this one, which is the plain sense of the phrase.

entries.clue: Here, so near the drinks (2,5)

indicatorNotes.drinks: To drink something in is to take it inside you, so the words in front are holding a run of letters within them.

blocks.note: seven letters running on across two gaps, the opening s and the closing e left behind

annotation.surface: Being pleasantly close to where the drinks are.
annotation.walkthrough: The run starts one letter into the first word and crosses two spaces, which is what keeps it out of sight. 'On earth' is also the phrase that follows 'what' or 'why' when a speaker is exasperated.
annotation.definitionFit: On earth means in this world and no other, so pointing at the ground we are standing on is exactly what 'here' does.

entries.clue: Partially shaven otter, poor wretch (4-3)

indicatorNotes.Partially: Partially means in part only, so a piece of what follows is taken and the rest of it left alone.

blocks.note: seven letters running on across the gap, leaving the s at the front and ter at the end

annotation.surface: A half-shorn otter, a sorry-looking animal.
annotation.walkthrough: A shaven otter is odd enough to look like the joke rather than the hiding place, which is the whole of the misdirection. The old division of society is into the haves and the have-nots.
annotation.definitionFit: A have-not is one of those with nothing in that division of rich from poor, so the phrase names a person the world has left out.

entries.clue: Clive, he reinvented scooter? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: A scooter is one kind of vehicle rather than a synonym for it, and the question mark is the setter owning up to defining by example.

indicatorNotes.reinvented: Something reinvented is put together differently from before, and letters reinvented arrive in a new order.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, a first name and a pronoun

annotation.surface: A man called Clive who has redesigned a scooter.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma turns the name into someone being addressed, which is enough to stop the two words looking like spare letters. Sir Clive Sinclair, who gave Britain the battery-driven C5, is the Clive the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A scooter is one machine among many that carry people about, and a vehicle is the general word for all of them.

entries.clue: Scar I've ruptured - showing these? (7)

indicatorNotes.ruptured: A ruptured thing has burst apart at the seam, and letters burst apart go back together differently.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing

annotation.surface: Somebody whose old scar has torn open.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'showing these' look like an afterthought when it is the definition, pointing at the answer instead of naming it. Every word of the clue is doing both jobs at once.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: viscera are the organs of the abdomen, and a scar torn open is the moment they would be on show.

entries.clue: Rose must have 'dealt with' rodent (7,5)

indicatorNotes.dealt with: Cards dealt out come round in whatever order they fall, so what is dealt with here is redistributed.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, a name and two verbs

annotation.surface: Rose being held responsible for getting rid of a mouse.
annotation.walkthrough: The inverted commas nudge 'dealt with' towards the euphemism for killing, and that is only the picture; underneath it is an instruction. The harvest mouse is the smallest British rodent, and it nests in standing corn.
annotation.definitionFit: The harvest mouse is a thumb-sized field mouse of English cornfields, and a mouse is a rodent, so the bare family name covers it.

entries.clue: Fish complain (4)

blocks.note: the heavy, long-lived freshwater fish of lakes and estate ponds
the verb, and a persistent one: to go on finding fault over something small

annotation.surface: Fish lodging a grievance.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, and no indicator anywhere to say where one stops. To carp is to keep finding fault over something small.
annotation.definitionFit: The carp is the heavy pond fish anglers sit all night for, and to carp is to grumble on and on, two unconnected words sharing a spelling.

entries.clue: Peel fruit on the radio (4)

indicatorNotes.on the radio: What comes over the radio is heard and never seen, so the word wanted is the one that merely sounds like this.

blocks.note: the fruit is a pear, and spoken aloud it is indistinguishable from the other spelling

annotation.surface: Peeling a piece of fruit with the radio on.
annotation.walkthrough: Two four-letter words, the same sound, no letter in common order: that is the whole clue. To pare a potato is to take the skin off it in thin strips.
annotation.definitionFit: To pare an apple is to peel it, working the knife round the skin, so the two verbs name one job.

entries.clue: Asian bear swimming around a body of water (7,3)

indicatorNotes.swimming around: A creature swimming around is circling with no settled course, and letters moving like that finish somewhere else.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder
the article is drawn into the fodder as its tenth letter

annotation.surface: A bear from Asia paddling round a lake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like the word that would put one thing inside another; here it belongs to the swimming, and the article after it is fodder. The Arabian Sea is the arm of the Indian Ocean between India and Oman.
annotation.definitionFit: The Arabian Sea is open salt water washing the coasts of India, Pakistan and Arabia, so 'body of water' is the category it sits in.

entries.clue: So, thyme regularly found to be ocular irritant (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Taken regularly means at a fixed interval, so every other letter is picked out and the ones between are passed over.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the two words run together

annotation.surface: Thyme being blamed, time and again, for making eyes sore.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'So' is the trap, because the count runs straight through it and treats both words as one string. A stye is the little abscess on the eyelid, and it is also spelt sty.
annotation.definitionFit: A stye is the inflamed swelling that comes up on an eyelid, which is irritation of the eye in the most literal sense.

entries.clue: Now, Christmas, for example ... (7,3)

annotation.definitionNote: Christmas is no example of the present day in the usual sense; the second reading takes the answer as two words, a day for presents, which is why 'for example' is there.

blocks.note: the ordinary sense, the era we happen to be living through
the second reading takes the two words apart: 25 December is a day on which parcels are handed over

annotation.surface: A speaker pausing in the middle of a list of occasions.
annotation.walkthrough: The trailing dots invite you to wait for the rest of the sentence when nothing more is coming. Splitting the answer into its two words is what turns 25 December into an instance of it.
annotation.definitionFit: The present day is the time we are living in, which is now; read as a day of presents, Christmas is the example the clue offers.

entries.clue: Make alterations to the battered safari suit at last (4)

indicatorNotes.at last: At last points to the back of the queue, so each word hands over only the letter it finishes on.

blocks.note: four words in the order printed, each giving up its final letter

annotation.surface: Finally getting round to altering a shabby old safari suit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At last' reads as relief that the job is happening and is the instruction that picks the letters. A safari suit is the four-pocketed cotton jacket and trousers of 1970s holiday photographs.
annotation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to make alterations to it, cutting and rewording until it reads as it should.
